metadata.title: Psychometric Framework for Modeling Parental Involvement and Reading Literacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study conducts secondary analyses of PIRLS-2011 data across 41 countries, using a three-level structure (student, school, country). The provided text does not report the use of PIRLS sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), nor does it name a weight variable (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT). Because the analysis is based on multilevel psychometric/latent regression modeling rather than ML algorithms, the manuscript’s weighting strategy is not documented in the excerpt; therefore, it is unclear whether complex survey design weights were applied. The analytic sample is described at the level of available student, school, and parent data per country, but no additional preprocessing filters (e.g., grade restrictions beyond grade 4, missing-data rules) are specified in the excerpt.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study’s core outcomes and modeling are based on PIRLS reading literacy and parental involvement constructs using IRT-based psychometric modeling (e.g., GPCM/bi-factor GPCM and multilevel latent regression), rather than reporting an explicit PV-based achievement modeling workflow (e.g., PVs with Rubin’s combining rules). As a result, plausible-value handling is not applicable to the extracted methodological description. The excerpt also does not specify how missing data were handled (e.g., complete-case vs imputation), representing a reporting gap for missingness strategy in the multilevel/IRT estimation context.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS-2011 secondary data with student, school, and parent information available for each of the 41 participating countries; analyses focus on grade 4 reading literacy and parental involvement components derived from PIRLS background questionnaires. The excerpt does not report additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., specific item-response completeness thresholds or missing-data exclusions), so the analytic sample is described only as the available PIRLS-2011 grade-4 dataset with the required questionnaire components.

data.outcome_summary: This chapter develops a psychometric framework linking parental involvement to PIRLS-2011 reading literacy, explicitly modeling cultural differential item functioning (CDIF) using IRT-based approaches (GPCM and bi-factor GPCM) and then assessing associations via three-level multilevel analyses (student, school, country). Across 41 countries, the random-intercept multilevel results indicate a rather weak but positive relationship between early literacy activities and grade-4 reading literacy after controlling for student gender and SES, while helping with homework shows a small negative effect. The authors conclude that CDIF did not influence the country-mean estimates or the latent regression outcomes, supporting international validity of the parental involvement scales despite some component reliability issues. When all five parental involvement components were included, the model explained approximately 15% at the student level, 46% at the school level, and 69% at the country level; the impact of helping with homework varied substantially across countries. The excerpt does not report PV-combining procedures or a missing-data handling strategy, and it cautions that PIRLS is cross-sectional, so causality cannot be claimed.
